args.query: What ImageNet/ILSVRC'15 top-5 error does the original ResNet paper report for its ensemble, and on which data split and evaluation protocol?
What single-crop and 10-crop top-5 errors does DenseNet report for DenseNet-201, and on which data split and model/evaluation setup?
Do the reported ResNet and DenseNet numbers use comparable training data, crop/ensemble protocols, and validation/test splits, or are they not like-for-like?

args.instructions: Answer the question directly in the first sentence. Then compare what each paper says, naming the paper for every point, and state where the papers agree, disagree or report numbers that are not comparable. If one hop of the question is not answered by the evidence, say which.

result.answer:
Answer: ResNet’s ILSVRC'15 ensemble top-5 error is 3.57% on the ImageNet test set; DenseNet-201 reports 6.34% single-crop and 5.54% 10-crop top-5 error on the ImageNet validation set. No—these numbers cannot establish a like-for-like head-to-head advantage.

The ResNet paper (1512.03385v1) Table 5 lists ResNet (ILSVRC'15) at 3.57, and its caption says the top-5 error is on the test set of ImageNet and reported by the test server [S:43eecbafc161#53]. That table reports error rates of ensembles [S:43eecbafc161#53], so the 3.57% is an ensemble, test-set result; the paper separately says it uses standard 10-crop testing for comparison studies [S:43eecbafc161#28].

The DenseNet paper (1608.06993v5) Table 3 gives DenseNet-201 top-5 errors of 6.34 / 5.54, which its caption defines as single-crop / 10-crop testing [S:20e50960076d#48], and the caption says these are top-1 and top-5 error rates on the ImageNet validation set [S:20e50960076d#48]. DenseNet's ImageNet setup uses the ILSVRC 2012 classification dataset with 1.2 million training images and 50,000 validation images from 1,000 classes; it applies a single 224x224 crop or 10 crops at test time and reports classification errors on the validation set [S:20e50960076d#46]. DenseNet also says it replaced the ResNet model with DenseNet-BC and kept all experiment settings exactly the same as those used for ResNet [S:20e50960076d#66], while noting that its hyperparameter settings were optimized for ResNets, not DenseNets [S:20e50960076d#67].

Thus the ResNet 3.57% is an ILSVRC'15 ensemble measured on the test server's test set, whereas DenseNet-201's 6.34%/5.54% are single-model validation results under single-crop/10-crop evaluation. The different split (test vs validation) and protocol (ensemble vs single model/crop) mean these reported numbers are not a matched comparison and do not establish a like-for-like head-to-head advantage.

citations.title: arXiv:1512.03385v1  [cs.CV]  10 Dec 2015
citations.text:
Our implementation for ImageNet follows the practice
in [21, 41]. The image is resized with its shorter side ran-
domly sampled in [256, 480] for scale augmentation [41].
A 224×224 crop is randomly sampled from an image or its
horizontal ﬂip, with the per-pixel mean subtracted [21]. The
standard color augmentation in [21] is used. We adopt batch
normalization (BN) [16] right after each convolution and
before activation, following [16]. We initialize the weights
as in [13] and train all plain/residual nets from scratch. We
use SGD with a mini-batch size of 256. The learning rate
starts from 0.1 and is divided by 10 when the error plateaus,
and the models are trained for up to 60 × 104 iterations. We
use a weight decay of 0.0001 and a momentum of 0.9. We
do not use dropout [14], following the practice in [16].
In testing, for comparison studies we adopt the standard

We simply replace the ResNet model with the DenseNet-

We report the single-crop and 10-crop validation errors

Figure 3 shows
the single-crop top-1 validation errors of DenseNets and
ResNets as a function of the number of parameters (left) and
FLOPs (right). The results presented in the ﬁgure reveal that
DenseNets perform on par with the state-of-the-art ResNets,
whilst requiring signiﬁcantly fewer parameters and compu-
tation to achieve comparable performance. For example, a
DenseNet-201 with 20M parameters model yields similar
validation error as a 101-layer ResNet with more than 40M
parameters. Similar trends can be observed from the right
panel, which plots the validation error as a function of the
number of FLOPs: a DenseNet that requires as much com-
